`pre-agent-aegis-guard.sh` gains `spec-checker` in its exempt list. The
nested-child transport-file band-aid is removed from `verify-spec` too.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep nesting + rely on the transport-file band-aid**: rejected — it
  failed a third time (the 40-minute stuck review). The band-aid addresses
  verdict *loss* but not the middle agent *hanging* on its child.
- **Fold find and verify into one agent (self-verify)**: rejected — destroys
  the independence that empirically refutes ~25–30% of candidates.
- **Fold both into the parent session (parent finds and verifies inline)**:
  rejected for the ADR-0011 reason — the parent is not implementation-blind;
  the bias check requires fresh contexts. Parent *orchestration* of two fresh
  agents is different and acceptable.

## Consequences

- The fragile depth-2 wait is gone; both dispatches are depth-1 the parent
  waits on directly.
- Unnesting made `review-verifier` an independently-dispatchable named agent,
  which would have let a verifier completion stamp the gate without a finder
  having run (and left mid-window edits invisible). The `.finder-done`
  diff-hash marker closes both: the stamp is provably downstream of a finder
  pass on the current diff. This restores the ADR-0011 property that a stamp
  cannot exist without a completed find pass.
- The parent's context now holds the candidate list and the verdicts (a few
  KB) — the cost ADR-0011 avoided by nesting. Negligible at this project's
  diff sizes; revisit if reviews of very large diffs make it material.
- Two agents per review instead of one-plus-child — same agent count, flatter
  shape.
- A model-tier change to `code-reviewer` or `review-verifier`, or a
  load-bearing edit to `review-diff`, requires a scored eval run
  (`scripts/evals/review-diff/`, ADR-0014). This change itself is
  validated that way.
- `verify-spec` is flattened the same way (`spec-verifier` hunter +
  `spec-checker`), resolving the debt this ADR would otherwise have left. A
  seeded-counterexample fixture under `scripts/evals/verify-spec/`
  exercises the flat spec pipeline end-to-end.

documents.title: Src Directory Layering
documents.content:
# 0016. `src/` is layered: routes → server functions → gateways → entities

- Status: accepted (amended 2026-08-13)
- Date: 2026-07-25

> **Amended 2026-08-13** — the deferred lint-rule alternative and the known
> request-context gap below are resolved. `arch-rules/layer-boundaries` now
> rejects route imports of the session adapter and Cloudflare bindings, and
> rejects gateway imports of auth adapters. `fetchCurrentUser()` takes the
> server-derived user id and email instead of resolving a session; the
> `getCurrentUser` server-only helper owns that resolution. The avatar HTTP route
> delegates authorization to `src/server/fn/avatar.ts`, which passes an
> ownership-validated key to `src/gateways/avatar/` for the R2 read. The rule's
> targeted tests, whole-project lint and typecheck, full test suite, and the
> Workers production build all passed after the change. The original Decision and
> Consequences remain as the record of the state this amendment replaced.

## Context

The repository already had a consistent layering — routes call server
functions, server functions call gateways, gateways own persistence — and the
2026-07-25 repo audit found **zero** violations of it. It also found that the
layering is documented nowhere: no ADR, no AGENTS.md section, no rule file. The
only occurrence of `gateways` in AGENTS.md is an example path inside the Aegis
instructions.

That makes the architecture invisible to the next contributor. An agent adding
a feature cannot tell whether a shortcut — a route importing a gateway
directly, a gateway reading the request context — is forbidden or merely
unused so far. Worse, the one document that did discuss module organization
(`.claude/rules/react.md`) named shared directories that do not exist in this
repo (`_ui/`, `_utils/`, `_repositories/`), so following it produced wrong
placements.

## Decision

`src/` has the following layers. Imports flow **downward only**; same-layer
imports are allowed, upward imports are not.

- **`src/routes/**`** — TanStack Router route modules and plain API routes. May
  import server functions, components, and entities. Must not import gateways
  or `src/lib/drizzle/**` directly.
- **`src/server/fn/**`** — server functions (`createServerFn`). This is the
  **authorization boundary**: resolve the session here and pass a
  server-derived user id downward. Never accept a caller-supplied identity.
- **`src/gateways/**`** — the only layer that touches persistence (D1 via
  Drizzle, R2). Never imports components. **Every mutation takes the identity
  as a parameter** — `updateUser` and `updateUserAvatar` receive a `userId`, and
  no gateway function accepts a caller-supplied one; that is the part the
  security property depends on. Reads are not there yet:
  `fetchCurrentUser()` calls `getSession()` itself, so the request context does
  reach this layer today. Stated as it is rather than as intended — see the
  Consequences.
- **`src/entities/**`** — domain types and Zod schemas. Imports nothing from
  the layers above.
- **`src/components/**`** — presentation. `features/<feature>/` for domain UI,
  `shared/<name>/` for cross-feature UI, `ui/` for shadcn CLI output (which
  must not be renamed — `components.json` aliases resolve to it).
- **`src/lib/**`** — framework and infrastructure adapters (auth, drizzle,
  storage) plus generic values with no component affinity.

`.claude/rules/react.md` carries the module-placement rules that agents read
per-file; this ADR carries the layer contract and the rationale.

## Alternatives considered

- **Leave it implicit**: rejected — an unwritten convention holds only while
  authorship stays consistent. The audit confirmed compliance today, which is
  evidence the convention is good, not evidence it is safe unwritten.
- **Record it only in AGENTS.md**: rejected — the Aegis knowledge base carries
  ADRs (ADR-0008), so an ADR with a `path_requires` edge on `src/**/*` is what
  actually surfaces to an agent editing those files. AGENTS.md gets a pointer,
  not the contract.
- **Enforce it with a lint rule**: not now — this needs an import-boundary rule
  wired into the oxlint config, and the convention has never been tested
  against a case that wants to bend. Deferred; the review pipeline is the check
  until then.
- **Collapse `server/fn` into `gateways`**: rejected — merging them would put
  session resolution next to SQL, and the audit's strongest positive finding
  was precisely that every mutation derives its user id from the session in a
  layer above persistence.

## Consequences

- The authorization boundary has a documented home, so a reviewer can name a
  violation instead of arguing style.
- New features have an unambiguous placement answer, and `react.md`'s examples
  now match reality.
- Cost: a genuine need to bypass a layer requires amending this ADR rather than
  just writing the import.
- The layering is **not** mechanically enforced. Nothing fails if it is
  violated; only the review pipeline catches drift. If a violation is ever
  found in review, that is the signal to revisit the lint-rule alternative.
- **One known gap, recorded rather than smoothed over.** An earlier draft of this
  ADR claimed gateways never read the request context. They do:
  `fetchCurrentUser()` resolves the session inside `src/gateways/user/`, so the
  read path couples that layer to the request. An external reviewer caught the
  overstatement — and the audit that produced this ADR had missed it, because it
  checked import direction (no route imports a gateway, no gateway imports a
  component) and never asked whether a gateway reads the session.
  Closing it means moving session resolution into `src/server/fn/` and passing
  the resolved user downward, which is a refactor with its own review rather
  than an edit to this ADR. Acceptance test: `src/gateways/` contains no import
  of `@/lib/auth/session`. Until then the boundary is real for mutations and
  aspirational for reads, and this ADR says so.

documents.title: Secret Value Boundary
documents.content:
# 0017. The boundary is the secret's value, not access to the file holding it

- Status: accepted
- Date: 2026-07-25

## Context

ADR-0004 made `permissions.deny`
the security boundary, and ADR-0013
added a `PreToolUse(Bash)` guard for the case prefix matching cannot express
("any command touching a file"). ADR-0004's 2026-07-25 amendment then narrowed
the `allow` list after finding that allow-listed readers walked around the deny
entries — and closed by *accepting* the remaining porosity: `cat .*`,
`grep -r . .` and similar still reach protected files without naming them, and
blocking those spellings was judged a poor trade because it misfires on ordinary
work while costing an attacker one more spelling.

That acceptance did not survive the day it was written. It also understated one
path: `cp`/`mv` sit in `ask`, and `ask` collapses into effective `allow` under
`acceptEdits` / `bypassPermissions` / auto mode — ADR-0004's own founding
argument, applied to itself.

Three subagents reached the protected files during a single audit session. All
three had been briefed in writing never to read them:

1. One built quote-split spellings (`c''at`) to defeat the lexical match.
2. One copied a protected file elsewhere with `cp` and read the copy.
3. One ran a repo-wide `grep -rn <name> .` while tracing where a variable was
   consumed. The protected file matched and its contents entered that agent's
   context; it self-reported, judging the value to look real. The owner
   confirmed it was a development placeholder, so nothing needed rotating — but
   that outcome came from what the file happened to hold, not from any control.

The harness flagged the first two. The third is decisive: it was not a
circumvention at all, but a correct, unremarkable command any contributor would
run. No regex tightening survives that case without breaking the work itself.

That also yields a rule worth stating plainly, because it generalises past this
project: **an instruction is not a control.** Telling an agent — in a briefing,
a skill, or a rule file — not to touch something constrains nothing. Only the
deny list and the hooks constrain, and both operate on spellings.

## Decision

Production secrets are never present in the working tree, so that reading one is
not a capability worth having.

- Real values live only in `wrangler secret put` (see `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md`).
  They are never written to a file, not even temporarily.
- Local env files carry development placeholders only. `.env.local.example` is
  the canonical list of *names*; a working copy holds dummy *values*.
- ADR-0004's `Read`/`Edit` deny entries and ADR-0013's guard hook stay, as
  defense-in-depth against accidental exposure. They raise the cost of a mistake
  and keep routine agent work from casually printing these files. They are not
  treated as a barrier against a determined path.
- Anything that would require a real secret on disk — a production-credentialed
  local run, a migration against a live database with its token in a file — is
  out of scope for an agent-driven session. Do it outside one.

**One standing exception: the drizzle-kit token.** `drizzle.config.ts` reads
`CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`, `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`, and
`CLOUDFLARE_D1_DATABASE_ID` from the local env file for drizzle-kit's `d1-http`
driver, which backs `db:push` / `db:generate` / `db:pull` / `db:studio`. That is
a real credential on disk, and the driver speaks HTTP with no access to
wrangler's authenticated session, so this decision cannot simply be asserted
over it. Conditions:

- The token carries **D1 edit only**. `docs/DATABASE_SETUP.md` used to walk the
  reader through granting Workers R2 Storage edit as well; nothing in the repo
  consumes that permission (the bucket and its public URL are dashboard
  configuration), so that instruction was narrowed alongside this ADR. The
  mitigation *is* the scope, so the scope has to be real rather than asserted.
- The four scripts are never unattended: `db:push` and `db:generate` have
  explicit `ask` entries; `db:pull` / `db:studio` reach `ask` through the default
  fallthrough for unlisted `bun run` targets. Gating the `bun run` wrapper is not
  enough on its own — `Bash(drizzle-kit generate:*)` was allow-listed, so the
  underlying binary ran unconfirmed and made this condition false for the
  equivalent command. It is in `ask` now. The general rule from ADR-0004's
  amendment applies: an entry that reaches the same capability by another
  spelling voids the gate on the first one.
- Its presence is temporary — remove or rotate the token when the remote-schema
  work is done, rather than leaving it in place between tasks.
- Closing the exception means not needing a static token. Direction, not a
  settled answer: `d1-http` takes an explicit token with no known path to
  wrangler's session, so closing this likely means driving remote schema changes
  through a wrangler-authenticated path instead of drizzle-kit, or wrapping it.
  Acceptance test either way: the remote path works with the token slot empty.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep ADR-0004's acceptance as written**: rejected — it was a prediction about
  attacker cost, and three incidents in one session falsified it. Leaving it
  would document a boundary the project does not actually have.
- **Extend the guard to block dotfile globs and recursive reads**: rejected. The
  third incident was `grep -rn`, which is ordinary work; a pattern broad enough
  to catch it breaks everyday searching, and a narrower one is defeated by the
  next spelling.
- **Scan command output for secret-shaped strings** (`PostToolUse(Bash)`):
  rejected in ADR-0004's amendment and still rejected — lexical in the same way,
  and it fires after the value is already in the transcript. Detection, not
  prevention.
- **Move `cp`/`mv` to `deny`**: rejected — they are needed for ordinary file
  work, and `deny` on them would not stop directory-level or archive-based
  reads. The same spelling problem one level out.

## Consequences

- The failure mode this accepts is narrow: an agent session can read development
  placeholders, and — until the exception closes — a least-privilege D1 token
  while remote schema work is in flight.
- The failure mode it removes is the one that matters: an application secret
  whose leak cannot be undone by tightening a regex afterwards.
- Nothing here is mechanically enforced. The conditions on the exception are
  prose, and no gate checks whether a file holds a real value or a placeholder.
  This ADR trades an unenforceable claim about access for an unenforceable claim
  about content — the difference is that the second one degrades gracefully:
  when it is violated, what leaks is a dummy.
- `wrangler secret put` becomes the only supported path for application secrets,
  so onboarding and rotation both route through `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md`.

documents.title: Compatibility Date Tracks Installed Workerd
documents.content:
# 0018. `compatibility_date` tracks the installed workerd, not today's date

- Status: accepted
- Date: 2026-07-28

## Context

`compatibility_date` in `wrangler.toml` selects the Workers runtime behaviour
this project opts into. Cloudflare's guidance is to set it to the current date
when starting a project and to update it occasionally, and it holds old dates
forever — so a stale date is not a fault that any gate reports. This project's
date sat at `2024-12-01` from the Next.js era through the TanStack Start
migration (ADR-0007), which the 2026-07-25
repo audit recorded as its last open item.

The obvious reading of "set it to the current date" is wrong here, and the
failure is not graceful. The local runtime is the `workerd` binary that comes in
with `wrangler`, and it refuses to start when the config asks for a date newer
than that binary supports:

```
service core:user:t: This Worker requires compatibility date "2026-07-28",
but the newest date supported by this server binary is "2026-07-15".
```

That is an error, not a warning — `vite dev` dies for everyone on the project,
while `wrangler deploy` would have been fine, because Cloudflare's edge runs a
current runtime. So the ceiling is a property of the installed toolchain, and it
does not track the calendar: with `wrangler` 4.110.0 / `workerd` 1.20260708.1 it
is `2026-07-15`, ahead of the workerd package's own version date.

The bump also flips every compatibility flag whose default date falls in the
skipped window: 44 flags carrying their own date, plus 27 that `nodejs_compat`
implies, which this project enables. Most are inert here (no Durable Objects, Queues,
Workflows, Containers, or Python; the app code uses no WebSocket, Cache API,
`URLPattern`, timers, `node:` imports, or `AsyncLocalStorage`), and
`assets_navigation_prefers_asset_serving` needs an `assets.not_found_handling`
that the generated deploy config does not set. The one flag that reaches this
codebase is `nodejs_compat_populate_process_env` (default from 2025-04-01),
which is why `src/lib/auth/auth.ts` and `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md` had to be corrected
alongside the date.

## Decision

`compatibility_date` is pinned to **the newest date the installed `workerd`
supports**, not to today's date. Raising it is part of raising `wrangler` — the
two move together, and the ceiling is discovered from the runtime rather than
assumed: set the date, run `bun run dev`, and read the error, which names the
supported date. `bun run cf-typegen` follows every change per
ADR-0005, and the flag deltas for
the skipped window are enumerated from `compatibility-date.capnp` in
`cloudflare/workerd`, which carries every flag's `compatEnableDate` and
`impliedByAfterDate` annotation in one machine-readable file. Cloudflare's flags
page documents the same flags, but one prose section per flag — which answers
"what does this flag do", not "what changed between these two dates".

## Alternatives considered

- **Today's date, per Cloudflare's starting-a-project guidance**: rejected — it
  breaks the local runtime, and the breakage is invisible until someone runs
  `dev`. The guidance is written for the case where the toolchain is current.
- **Bump `wrangler` first so the ceiling reaches today**: rejected as part of
  this change, not in general. `@cloudflare/vite-plugin`'s `peerDependencies`
  pin a `wrangler` floor that climbs with each plugin release, so the two are
  bumped in lockstep as their own ticket.
- **Leave the date alone, since Cloudflare supports old dates forever**:
  rejected — new features are gated on a current date, and the gap only ever
  grows, so the eventual bump reviews more flag changes at once.
- **Pin flags explicitly instead of leaning on the date's defaults**: rejected —
  it duplicates the runtime's own defaults into config that then needs its own
  maintenance, for a project whose surface the flags do not touch.

## Consequences

- The date is bounded by the toolchain, so it can lag the calendar. That is
  intended: the number states which runtime the project has actually been run
  against, which a calendar date does not.
- A `wrangler` bump now has a second step (re-check the ceiling, move the date)
  and a review obligation (the flags in the newly crossed window).
- `process.env` is populated from text bindings from now on. Nothing in the app
  reads it, and better-auth's secret still arrives explicitly, but code that
  starts depending on `process.env` would be depending on a flag default.
- Verified for this bump: `typecheck`, 135 tests, `build`, and a `dev` smoke
  test of `/`, `/profile`, and better-auth's session endpoint.

documents.title: Single Pass Review
documents.content:
# 0019. The review is one pass: find → verify → fix → done

- Status: accepted
- Date: 2026-07-28

## Context

ADR-0013 made any `Edit`/`Write`
clear `.claude/.review-stamp`, so fixing a finding required reviewing again
before committing. That closed a real hole — the old stamp proved only "a review
happened at some point" — and it was judged affordable because
ADR-0011 had dropped a review
to two agents.

The cost was then measured and found high, not affordable:
ADR-0014 recorded re-reviews
re-reading the full diff and re-running whole-project verification the parent had
already run (~40–105k tokens, 1–5 min per run). Its remedy was to make the second
review cheap (delta mode, −62% tool uses) rather than to remove it.

Two sessions of operating that answer show it does not hold:

- **Delta mode does not get used.** It is an instruction, not a mechanism.
  On 2026-07-28 the parent ran full-mode re-reviews instead, and separately
  fixed findings before dispatching the verifier — which broke the diff-hash
  pairing and cost an entire extra find+verify pair. Both are the failure mode
  ADR-0001 named: guidance that depends on the agent choosing to follow it.
- **The user experience is the loop, not the token count.** What the repository
  owner reported was watching the verifier start again after every fix. A
  procedure with a return arrow reads as unbounded even when each iteration is
  cheap, and it makes the reviewer feel like a toll rather than a check.

Meanwhile the exposure ADR-0013 was closing is now covered from other
directions. The Stop gate runs typecheck / lint / format / knip / similarity on
the post-fix tree; lefthook checks staged files with `--check` only, precisely so
the committed bytes equal the reviewed bytes; CI re-runs typecheck, lint, format,
knip, test and build on the PR (not similarity — that check is local-only); and
an independent PR-side AI reviewer (cubic) reads the final diff — including the
fixes — before merge. What a second local review adds is judgment on the fix
itself, and only that.

## Decision

The pre-commit review is **one pass: find → verify → fix → done**. Fixing what
the verifier confirmed does not trigger another review — `post-edit-check.sh` no
longer clears `.review-stamp`, so those edits keep it and the parent commits
next. This amends ADR-0013's review-gate bullet; the rest of ADR-0013 (gates as
deterministic artifacts) is untouched, and this is deliberately a return to
ADR-0009's original reasoning, which rejected
diff binding because "strict diff binding would force a re-review after every
fix".

Removing the per-edit clear takes away more than the loop: that clear was also
what stopped one task's stamp from authorising the next task's commit. The first
draft of this ADR claimed the remaining clears (a `code-reviewer` dispatch, an
aegis cycle) covered that, "which every new task must run" — an instruction, not
a mechanism, and the review of this very change reproduced the hole end-to-end:
task A reviewed, fixed and committed, then an unrelated never-reviewed task B
committed on task A's stamp, because a parent implementing directly (ADR-0012)
triggers neither clear. One mechanism replaces it:

**A commit that leaves the working tree clean consumes the stamp**
(`post-bash-stamp-consume.sh`). One review still covers a multi-commit split,
because the tree stays dirty between partial commits; once the reviewed batch is
fully landed, the stamp has nothing left to authorise and the next task starts
without one.

Two properties are unchanged: the `.finder-done` diff-hash marker from
ADR-0015 still means editing *between* the two
dispatches yields no stamp and a lone verifier cannot stamp, and the two
pre-existing clears still fire.

**Delta mode is deleted**, not demoted. It existed to make the second review
cheap; with no second review it is dead weight, and a mode that must be
remembered is the failure mode this ADR is correcting. `review-diff` now has one
mode, and the `mode` / `fallback` fields are gone from the finder and verifier
output contracts.

**Residual gap, stated rather than papered over.** No hook can decide "is this a
new task", so the mechanism keys on the observable proxy instead. A task boundary
crossed with leftover dirt in the tree (a scratch file, a deliberately deferred
hunk, an early draft of the next task) never reaches "clean", so the stamp
survives it and the follow-on work can commit unreviewed. The exposure is one
task deep and requires the parent to also skip the Aegis consult AGENTS.md
mandates. A scope check on the stamp would narrow it, and was built and then
removed during this change: it blocked a fix that *added* a file, which is a
re-review by another name and therefore the thing being removed. Narrowing this
gap is only worth doing with a mechanism that never blocks a fix.

`scripts/test-review-gate.py` drives these sequences against the real hooks in a
throwaway repository, so the behaviour above is executable rather than asserted.
Run it after touching `pre-bash-guard.sh`, `post-agent-review-stamp.sh`, or
`post-bash-stamp-consume.sh`.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep the loop and actually use delta mode**: rejected by the repository
  owner after the cost was explained. It also leaves the mechanism resting on
  the agent remembering to pick the cheap mode — the thing that already failed.
- **Re-run only the verifier on the fix (three agents)**: rejected — it is still
  a return arrow, which is what the owner objected to, and it would require
  loosening the ADR-0015 pairing invariant that makes the stamp meaningful.
- **Keep clearing, but only for edits outside the confirmed findings' files**:
  rejected — "was this edit part of the fix" is not decidable by a hook, and a
  gate that guesses is worse than one that is explicit about what it does not
  check.
- **Record the reviewed file scope in the stamp and block commits that grow it**:
  built during this change, then removed. It narrows the residual gap below, but
  a fix that extracts a helper into a new file is an ordinary fix, and blocking
  it is a re-review wearing different clothes.
- **Match the commit gate against a diff hash taken at stamp time**: rejected —
  it re-blocks after every fix, which is the loop verbatim. ADR-0013's own
  Alternatives had already rejected it for a different reason (multi-commit
  splits move `git diff HEAD`).
- **Record post-review edits in an artifact and disclose them at commit time**:
  rejected for now — it is a warning, and ADR-0013 already established that a
  warning the agent may ignore is not a gate. Revisit if fixes are found to
  introduce defects in practice.

## Consequences

- A review costs two agents, once, per commit. The return arrow is gone from
  AGENTS.md, `review-diff`, `start-workflow`, and `docs/agent-workflow.md`.
- **The fix itself is no longer judged by a fresh context.** This is the
  accepted risk, and it has a recorded precedent: the 2026-07-25 audit's S0
  entry describes a first fix that was incomplete (it passed the secret but left
  the absent case silent) and was caught by exactly the re-review this ADR
  removes. The mitigations are the Stop gate, CI, and the PR-side reviewer —
  none of which reason about intent. Fixes that are more than mechanical should
  therefore be re-reviewed by choice.
- Ordering discipline matters more than before: the only edits the stamp
  survives are the ones made *after* the verifier returns. Editing between
  finder and verifier still costs the whole pass.
- This amends ADR-0014's second
  decision, which added delta mode; that mode is now deleted. Its fixture and
  measurements in `scripts/evals/review-diff/` are kept as the record of
  why it existed, and are no longer exercised.
- ADR-0014's eval obligation covers "any load-bearing edit to `review-diff`".
  Nothing here changes how the finder or verifier judge a diff — the judging
  logic in Steps 1 and 3 is untouched, and only the output envelope in Steps 2
  and 4 lost the `mode` / `fallback` fields — so a scored run would reproduce the
  existing scores.
  Deleting a mode removes a code path rather than adding one to measure. No eval
  run was made; that is a scoping judgement, recorded so it can be disputed
  rather than discovered.
- Fixes that are more than mechanical now land unjudged by design. If that turns
  out to cost defects, the honest next move is the one the owner suggested during
  this change: make the single pass produce the fix — have the verifier return
  the concrete change and its acceptance check for each surviving finding — so
  the judgement happens inside the pass instead of after it.

documents.title: Verifier Returns The Fix
documents.content:
# 0020. The verifier returns the fix, not just the finding

- Status: accepted
- Date: 2026-07-28

## Context

ADR-0019 made the review one pass — find → verify →
fix → done — and recorded what that costs: "the fix itself is no longer judged by
a fresh context." The shape of the pipeline made the gap precise. The finder finds,
the verifier refutes, and then **the parent invents the remedy**, which nothing
downstream examines. The Stop gate, lefthook, CI and the PR-side reviewer all
check mechanics; none of them asks whether the change addresses the finding.

That gap is not theoretical. The 2026-07-25 audit's S0 entry records a first fix
that passed a secret explicitly but left the absent case silent — correct-looking,
incomplete, and caught only by the re-review ADR-0019 removed.

The repository owner named the move while ADR-0019 was still being written: if the
pass happens once, invest in making that one pass right. The cheapest place to
invest is the step that currently has no reviewer.

## Decision

For every finding it does not refute, the verifier also returns:

- **`fix`** — the concrete change: which file, what it should say instead, and why
  that shape rather than the alternative considered. A restatement of the problem
  does not qualify.
- **`acceptance`** — how the parent confirms the fix landed, checkable without
  re-running the review: a command, or a specific observable in the code.

The parent applies those and commits. Departing from a returned fix is allowed —
the parent can see things the verifier could not — but it must say so and why.

**Findings that need a decision are exempt, explicitly.** Where a remedy turns on
an ADR-level choice or a genuine trade-off, the verifier writes that in `fix`
along with the credible options instead of inventing one, and the parent asks the
user. Forcing a fix into every field would manufacture confident answers to
questions that belong to the owner — the opposite of the goal.

This does not reintroduce a return arrow. Nothing re-runs; the judgement moves
*into* the pass rather than after it.

## Alternatives considered

- **Re-run the verifier on the fix**: rejected in ADR-0019 and still rejected —
  it is the loop the owner objected to, in a smaller costume.
- **Treat the finder's proposed fix as final, unjudged**: rejected. The finder
  already sketches a fix per Step 1 — written before verification, for candidates
  that may not survive it — so treating that sketch as final would let an
  unverified remedy land. The verifier's `fix`, written only for survivors, after
  refutation, with the code loaded, supersedes it. (Removing the finder's
  obligation was not an option either: AGENTS.md requires findings to propose a
  concrete alternative.)
- **Have the parent write the fix and a separate agent judge it**: rejected — a
  third dispatch per review, for a judgement the verifier is already positioned
  to make while it has the code loaded.
- **Leave it to the parent and rely on the PR-side reviewer**: rejected. That
  reviewer sees the final diff without the finding that motivated it, so it cannot
  tell a complete fix from a plausible one.

## Consequences

- The verifier does more per finding, so its cost rises with the number of
  survivors. On a clean diff nothing changes: no survivors, no fixes.
- The first verifier to run under this contract hit a gap in it while following
  it: the decision-exemption path said what `fix` should hold but not
  `acceptance`, so it had to invent a convention. That is the kind of defect a
  contract only reveals in use, and it is why the contract was exercised on its
  own diff before being committed.
- **The risk is attention, not correctness.** A verifier asked to design remedies
  may refute less rigorously — the failure would show up as false positives
  surviving, or as expected findings missed. That is exactly what the golden evals
  measure, which is why this change is gated on a scored run rather than argued.
- The parent's latitude is narrowed on purpose: it applies a judged fix instead of
  authoring an unjudged one. The escape hatch is disclosure, not silence.
- `mode` / `fallback` were already gone from the return contract (ADR-0019); this
  adds `fix` and `acceptance` to it. Consumers of the report are the parent and
  the human reading it, so the shape can change without a migration.
- Under ADR-0014 this is a
  load-bearing edit to `review-diff` that changes how the verifier behaves, so it
  required a scored eval run:
  `scripts/evals/review-diff/results/2026-07-29-verifier-returns-fix.md`.
  Four fixtures rather than eight, by agreement — detection, false positives on a
  clean diff, discrimination in a mixed diff, and scale. **4/4 found, 0 missed,
  0 false positives, cost flat against the 2026-07-12 baselines**, so the
  attention risk above did not materialise at this scale. What the run does *not*
  measure is the quality of `fix` / `acceptance` themselves: no fixture has an
  expected fix, so a correct detection with a degraded remedy would still score
  clean. That gap, and the four unrun fixtures, are recorded in the results file.
- Regenerating two stale fixtures for that run produced the more interesting
  result. The first rebuild of fx-08 contained three edits meant to be benign that
  were not — two asserted unverified facts about jsdom and better-auth, one broke
  the import-block convention — and the finder flagged all three, correctly,
  against the very rule the fixture author had skipped. The pipeline read the
  codebase more carefully than the person writing its test did.

documents.title: Records Live Only In The Knowledge Base
documents.content:
# 0021. Records live only in the knowledge base; `docs/adr/` and `docs/superpowers/` are removed

- Status: accepted (amended by 0023)
- Date: 2026-07-29

> **Note (ADR-0023, 2026-07-30):** the Consequence below stating that `expanded`
> context "is still inert" because `includes_tag_mappings` is `false` **no longer
> holds** — `aegis-share/source/tag-mappings.json` now populates the catalog and
> tag-driven expansion is verified working. The sentence is left as written because
> it records the state at the time of this decision. Every decision in this ADR
> stands unchanged.

## Context

Three directories held records of the same kind: `docs/adr/` (decisions),
`docs/superpowers/specs/` (design notes and audit findings) and
`docs/superpowers/plans/` (work plans). `docs/adr/` was additionally mirrored into
`aegis-share/source/documents/`, with AGENTS.md requiring every ADR edit to be
copied across and the share pipeline re-run, and a Stop-gate check watching for
the drift that discipline exists to prevent.

Measured on 2026-07-29: the process apparatus (`.claude/` 5,649 lines,
`docs/adr/` 1,818 lines, AGENTS.md, 34 files under `docs/superpowers/`) was
roughly three times the size of the application it governs (`src/`, 48 files,
2,506 lines), and 58 of the previous 60 non-merge commits touched only the
apparatus. The repository owner's objection was that the structure had become
the product.

ADR-0008 had already considered and rejected exactly the consolidation this ADR
makes — "keep detailed rules on disk, serve them via Aegis only: rejected —
deferred delivery requires readable source files". That premise no longer holds.
`aegis_compile_context` accepts `content_mode: "always"`, which returns every
document's body inline; verified the same day against knowledge_version 120,
where a request with that mode returned all seven matched documents with
content. The rejection was correct about the default and wrong about the tool.

Two further facts settled the mechanics. `aegis_sync_docs` documents
`skipped_invalid_anchor` for "unusable paths (missing, outside project, or
resolve errors)", so a deleted anchor is skipped rather than an error.
`aegis-share/canonical.json` carries each document's full `content`, so the
bundle is self-contained and deleting the anchored file loses nothing.

## Decision

**The knowledge base under `aegis-share/source/` is the only home for records.**

- `docs/adr/` and `docs/superpowers/` are deleted. The 20 ADRs already existed in
  `source/documents/`; nothing else in those trees was a record the project still
  acted on. `specs/` is **not** a record location and stays: a
  `specs/<feature>.spec.md` is a working file a task writes, verifies and then
  implements against, like the eval fixtures. Only its `README.md` is removed,
  because that was format documentation and now lives in the `verify-spec` skill.
- Every document becomes `ownership: standalone` with no `source_path`. Nothing
  anchors them any more, because nothing outside the knowledge base holds their
  text. Two other options were tried first and rejected by measurement: leaving
  the anchors pointing at the deleted `docs/adr/` paths makes every sync report
  `skipped_invalid_anchor`, and re-anchoring each document to its own
  `source/documents/adr-NNNN.md` makes all 21 permanently stale — that file
  carries frontmatter the stored body does not, so the hashes can never agree,
  and `aegis_sync_docs` opened an update proposal on the first document tried.
  A `doctor` that always reports attention is not a check (ADR-0013).
- Relative cross-links between ADR bodies (`](0015-flat-review-pipeline.md)`)
  became plain `ADR-0015` text. They only resolved while the files sat in one
  directory, and a link is navigation, not a claim.
- The Stop-gate Aegis check now watches `aegis-share/source/` instead of
  `docs/adr/`. Its subject moved; the failure it catches — editing the source and
  forgetting the pipeline — did not go away.
- The eval fixtures moved to `scripts/evals/`. They are patches and expected
  outputs, not records, and `scripts/` already holds their runners.
- `docs/adr/README.md`'s durable content — when an ADR is warranted, the
  MADR-lite skeleton, and the numbering rules — moved into AGENTS.md as
  "ADR form". Its index is not reproduced: the knowledge base is the list.
  `specs/README.md`'s spec skeleton moved the same way, into the `verify-spec`
  skill's own **Format** section, since that skill is its only consumer. The
  directory itself keeps its role — `start-workflow` step 4 still writes there.
- **Retired decisions stop being served.** Seven edges pointed at the four ADRs
  with no live decision (0001, 0003, 0009, 0010) and are removed: `review` and
  `.claude/hooks/**` reached 0009 while already reaching its successor 0011;
  `refactor` and `scaffold` reached 0003 alongside 0012; `specs/**` and `scaffold`
  both reached 0010, whose spec-verification mandate is stated unconditionally in
  AGENTS.md's Workflow section and gated by `start-workflow` step 4, so both edges
  were redundant rather than load-bearing — not removed because the path went away,
  since `specs/` stays; and `src/**/*` reached 0001 — the history of where rule
  files used to live, which a `src` edit does not need. The
  documents stay (numbering is never reused), but nothing resolves to them, so
  compiling context no longer hands the reader a decision that was replaced. It
  did before: a `review` compile on 2026-07-29 returned adr-0009's full body at
  relevance 0.56.
- **Work findings are not persisted.** `repo-audit`'s "Work" lane reported to
  `docs/superpowers/specs/`; with that directory gone the lane now reports to the
  user in the audit summary. Routing it into the knowledge base was considered and
  rejected — ADR-0008 item 2 restricts the KB to decisions and this ADR keeps that
  item, every document is `kind: reference`, and the plan directories were deleted
  because nothing had been acting on them.

This amends ADR-0008: decision item 2 ("the KB carries ADRs only") stands, and
its rejected "serve via Aegis only" alternative is now the chosen design.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep `docs/adr/` as the source and drop the `aegis-share/` pipeline**:
  rejected by the owner, who asked for the knowledge base to be the single home.
  It would also give up Aegis's relevance-ordered serving for a plain directory.
- **Keep both copies and live with the mirror discipline**: rejected — it is the
  status quo, and the Stop-gate check existed only because the discipline is
  forgettable.
- **Delete Aegis instead, and keep plain files**: proposed during the same
  session on the evidence that ten consultations had returned nothing unique.
  Withdrawn: that run passed `intent_tags: []` against an empty tag catalog and
  never requested inline content, so it measured a misconfiguration rather than
  the tool.

## Consequences

- One place to edit a record, and the share pipeline is the only step that can
  be forgotten. `doctor` reporting in_sync remains the check.
- A human browsing the repository no longer finds ADRs by reading a directory;
  they read `aegis-share/source/documents/` or ask Aegis. The frontmatter makes
  those files less pleasant to read than the ones they replace.
- `expanded` context is still inert: `manifest.json` records
  `includes_tag_mappings: false`, so `aegis_get_known_tags` returns an empty
  catalog and tag-driven expansion cannot fire. That is now the largest unused
  half of the tool, and it is a setup gap rather than a design decision.
- Older ADR bodies still describe paths that no longer exist (`docs/adr/`,
  `docs/superpowers/specs/`). Those sentences record where things were when the
  decision was made and are deliberately not rewritten; this ADR is the note
  that explains them.

documents.title: Review Stamp Keys On Subagent Completion
documents.content:
# 0022. The review stamp keys on `SubagentStop`, not on the dispatch returning

- Status: accepted (amended by 0029)
- Date: 2026-07-30

> **Amended by ADR-0029** (2026-08-07): this decision required **two**
> independent facts. The pairing half — that the parent did not edit between the
> two dispatches, recorded as `.finder-hash` and `.pair-ok` — is moot, because
> ADR-0029 leaves one dispatch and there is no between. The other half stands and
> is now the entire gate: the stamp keys on `SubagentStop` rather than on the
> dispatch returning, and refuses a blank `last_assistant_message`. The cost
> recorded below is the reason ADR-0029 was worth making.

## Context

ADR-0015 unnested the verifier and stated that **`review-verifier`'s completion
stamps the commit gate**. ADR-0019 rested the whole single-pass design on that
same sentence. The implementation never did it: `post-agent-review-stamp.sh` was
registered on `PostToolUse(Agent)`.

`PostToolUse` fires after a tool call *succeeds*, and the Agent tool's call
succeeds as soon as the subagent is launched — background execution has been the
platform default for subagents since Claude Code 2.1.198, and the tool returns
launch metadata rather than a result. Measured across this project's transcripts
on 2026-07-30: 122 Agent results, every one of them `status: "async_launched"`,
`isAsync: true`, with a body reading "Async agent launched successfully". The
harness has a separate event for what the ADRs meant — `SubagentStop`, "when a
subagent finishes" — carrying `agent_type`, `agent_id` and
`last_assistant_message`.

So the gate certified dispatch, not review. Launching `code-reviewer` wrote the
`.finder-done` diff hash and launching `review-verifier` wrote `.review-stamp`,
in both cases before either agent had read a line of the diff. Two Agent calls in
sequence unlocked `git commit`.

This was found by investigating a narrower symptom. On 2026-07-29 a
`review-verifier` stalled and produced no verdicts, yet the commit gate was
stamped; that was recorded as "the stamp hook does not check whether the dispatch
failed", and the intended fix was to copy the `tool_response.isError` check that
`post-aegis-compile.sh` already performs. That diagnosis was wrong in a way worth
recording: there was no error to detect. The launch had succeeded, which is all
`PostToolUse` was ever told about. A stalled verifier stamping the gate was not an
unhandled edge case — it was the mechanism working as wired.

ADR-0013 requires gates to key on deterministic artifacts rather than on trust in
the orchestrator. This gate did key on an artifact; the artifact just recorded the
wrong event.

## Decision

A stamp requires two independent facts. They are observable at different moments,
so **each is gathered where it is actually observable**, and the stamp requires
both:

| Fact | Where | Artifact |
|---|---|---|
| the parent did not edit between the two agents (ADR-0015 pairing) | between the finder's **completion** and the verifier's **dispatch** — the window the parent controls | `.finder-hash`, re-sampled and compared at the verifier's dispatch → `.pair-ok` |
| both agents actually finished | `SubagentStop` | `.finder-done`, then `.review-stamp` |

- **`post-agent-review-stamp.sh` moves to `SubagentStop`.** `code-reviewer`'s stop
  writes `.finder-done` and records `.finder-hash`; `review-verifier`'s stop writes
  `.review-stamp` only if `.finder-done` and `.pair-ok` both exist, then consumes
  the cycle's markers. The comparison itself lives in the new
  `pre-agent-review-pair.sh`, at the verifier's dispatch.
- **The compared window contains neither agent's own execution, and getting that
  right took three attempts.** Both review agents hold `Bash` and run experiments
  in the repository, so any window containing an agent's run is voided by that
  agent's own scratch files rather than by anything the parent did. Sampling at the
  verifier's *completion* included the verifier's run; sampling at the finder's
  *dispatch* included the finder's. Both failed against real reviews of this very
  change. `[finder completion, verifier dispatch]` includes neither. The shared
  `lib-review-hash.sh` holds the one hash definition, because two copies would be
  two chances for a drift that never fails loudly — it only refuses every commit.
- **A failed pairing says so, at the verifier's dispatch**, instead of surfacing as
  a commit refused minutes later with no stated cause.
- **Which role finished comes from the invocation argument, not the payload.**
  `.claude/settings.json` registers the stamp script twice, once per matcher
  (`code-reviewer` → `finder`, `review-verifier` → `verifier`), so the harness's own
  agent-type matching is the single place the mapping lives, and
  `scripts/test-review-gate.py` asserts that wiring against the real settings file.
  `agent_type` is read only as a fallback: 20 of 23 `SubagentStop` payloads captured
  on 2026-07-30 carried `agent_type: ""` (unrelated harness-internal subagents), so
  it is not a field to depend on — even though both pinned agents do populate it,
  which an earlier version of this ADR wrongly claimed they did not.
- **The hook refuses any other event.** If `hook_event_name` is not `SubagentStop`
  it writes no marker and warns, naming the event it got. A `PostToolUse` payload
  carries the agent's type under a different key, so a script reading either field
  would silently resume stamping at launch — one settings edit away, and this makes
  that edit loud instead of invisible.
- **The filename does not change.** ADR-0013, ADR-0015 and ADR-0019 each name
  `post-agent-review-stamp.sh`, and an ADR is never rewritten (AGENTS.md, "ADR
  form"), so a rename would leave three records citing a path that does not
  exist. The file's header states which event it is registered on.

The sidechain check is dropped from the stamp path. `SubagentStop` fires about a
child that stopped, so testing a transcript for `isSidechain` would either skip
every legitimate stamp or test nothing, and what it guarded is now moot: the four
pinned review agents hold no `Agent` tool, so a review cannot nest inside a
review. Both `PreToolUse` hooks keep their own check, where the reasoning (a review
launched from inside a subagent must not touch the parent's markers) still applies.

The two new markers, `.finder-hash` and `.pair-ok`, are added to `.gitignore`
in the same change. That is not housekeeping: an un-ignored marker enters the
working-tree hash, so writing it would change the value it is about to be compared
against, and the gate would never stamp.

`scripts/test-review-gate.py` drives dispatch and completion as separate events
through the real hooks, and pins what this decision turns on: a launch-shaped
payload writes no marker and reports the mis-registration; a verifier with no
finder dispatch cannot pair; a parent edit between the two dispatches breaks the
pairing and says so; and — the case the earlier design got wrong — **a file
appearing and disappearing inside the repository during an agent's own run leaves
the pairing intact.** It also asserts the `settings.json` matcher→role wiring
itself, because that mapping is exactly what no test previously covered.

This amends ADR-0015 and ADR-0019 on one point of fact: the sentence "its
completion stamps the commit gate" describes this ADR's implementation, not the
one those ADRs shipped with. Their reasoning is unchanged and was always written
against completion.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep `PostToolUse(Agent)` and inspect `tool_response`**: rejected, and it was
  the original plan. There is nothing in a successful launch response to inspect —
  no field distinguishes "this agent will produce a verdict" from "this agent will
  stall". The check would have looked like a fix and changed nothing.
- **Have the verifier write the stamp itself as its last action**: rejected — the
  agent would be certifying itself, and ADR-0013 exists because gates must not
  depend on an agent choosing to perform a step. It would also need `Write`,
  which the review agents deliberately lack.
- **Have the parent write the stamp after reading the verdicts**: rejected for the
  same reason one step further out. The parent is the party the gate constrains.
- **Poll for subagent completion from the `Stop` hook**: rejected — it reintroduces
  transcript inspection to answer a question `SubagentStop` answers directly.
- **Refuse to stamp when the verifier's `last_assistant_message` is blank**:
  built, then removed, and now known to be implementable. An agent that stopped
  without reporting has verified nothing, so the check is well-motivated. It was
  removed while the field's behaviour was unobserved, because this change had
  already shown what an unverified payload assumption costs and a gate that wedges
  every commit is worse than the narrow hole it closes. A `review-verifier` payload
  has since been captured carrying a 19,525-character `last_assistant_message`, so
  the objection no longer holds — but adding the check back belongs in its own
  change with its own validation, not bolted onto the one that removed it. That
  change landed on 2026-07-31; see the Residual gap consequence below for the shape
  it took.
- **Additionally require the verifier's report to parse as the expected verdict
  schema**: rejected. It makes the gate a content judge, and schema drift would
  then block every commit.

## Consequences

- The stamp now means what three ADRs already claimed it meant. A stalled,
  killed, or never-reporting verifier leaves the commit blocked.
- **The gate got strictly stricter, and existing habits may now block.** Any flow
  that dispatched the two agents and moved on without waiting for both to finish
  used to earn a stamp and no longer does. That flow was never valid — AGENTS.md
  already requires the parent to wait on both depth-1 dispatches — but it used to
  be silently survivable.
- Wiring correctness is self-testing: if the `SubagentStop` matcher does not fire,
  no stamp appears and the next commit is refused. The failure mode is a blocked
  commit, never a false pass.
- **Residual gap — closed 2026-07-31.** As written, `SubagentStop` proved an agent
  finished but not that it said anything, so a verifier that died mid-run still
  stamped if it stopped after a finder ran on the same diff. That happened on
  2026-07-30: a `review-verifier` died on an API 529 and the gate was stamped with
  no verdict. The blank-report check was then added — the verifier branch now
  refuses to stamp when `last_assistant_message` is present but blank, and stamps
  with a warning when the field is absent entirely, so a platform that does not
  supply it cannot wedge every commit. `scripts/test-review-gate.py` pins both
  outcomes. What remains open is narrower and unchanged: `SubagentStop` still cannot
  prove the agent produced a *real* review. The finder/verifier independence
  (ADR-0015) is what makes the report worth something, and that rests on the pinned
  agent definitions, not on this hook.
- **The lesson generalises past this hook.** `PostToolUse` was assumed to mean
  completion; then, while fixing that, `agent_type` was assumed to be populated for
  every relevant event — an assumption a later, larger capture only partially
  contradicts (populated for both pinned agents; genuinely empty on 20 unrelated
  events) without ever settling why the first version failed. Hook payload
  behaviour belongs in `scripts/test-review-gate.py` as cases built from captured
  payloads, not from the documentation's field list.
- **A hook script registered without the executable bit is silently dead**, and
  `pre-agent-review-pair.sh` shipped that way for one cycle: created 644 while every
  sibling is 755, so the harness — which invokes registered hooks by bare path —
  could not run it, `.pair-ok` never appeared, and no commit could be stamped. This
  is the "gate silently off" failure ADR-0013 exists to prevent, and
  `scripts/test-review-gate.py` masked it by construction, invoking hooks as
  `bash <path>`, which ignores mode bits. It now reads the real `settings.json` and
  asserts every project-local hook command is executable.
- **Cost, recorded because it was substantial.** Four review cycles: three failed to
  stamp, each for a different reason (the wrong event, then two wrong windows, plus
  the missing executable bit). None was wasted — they produced ten confirmed
  findings, several of them false claims this ADR's own author had written about the
  mechanism while changing it. The recurring fault was one habit: describing hook
  behaviour from documentation rather than from an observed payload or an executed
  path, then documenting the description instead of the behaviour.
- The 2026-07-29 memory note that framed this as a missing `isError` check is
  superseded by this ADR; the diagnosis, not just the fix, was wrong.

documents.title: Tag Mappings And Instruction Document Edges
documents.content:
# 0023. Tags reach what paths cannot; instruction documents get edges, not KB entries

- Status: accepted
- Date: 2026-07-30

> **Note (2026-07-30):** the Decision below states a tag count and list current as
> of its writing. `aegis-share/source/tag-mappings.json` is the live authority for
> which tags exist and how many — treat the Decision's numbers and list as a
> point-in-time snapshot, not a running total, and do **not** add another note like
> this one when tags are later added or removed; the reach test below is what
> governs each new mapping. (This note was itself prompted by adding a mapping
> under that test shortly after the ADR was written — and its first draft named the
> new ordinal, which would have gone stale on the next addition in exactly the way
> the Decision's count did.)

## Context

Two halves of Aegis were unused, both setup gaps rather than decisions.

ADR-0021 recorded the first as a Consequence: `manifest.json` had
`includes_tag_mappings: false`, so `aegis_get_known_tags` returned `[]` and the
`expanded` half of `aegis_compile_context` could never fire. Passing
`intent_tags: []` looked like a choice when it was the only available outcome —
which is how a 2026-07-29 session concluded that Aegis "returned nothing unique"
and proposed deleting it, having measured a misconfiguration rather than the tool.

The second was a `compile_miss` observation from the same day: no path edge
existed from `AGENTS.md` or `.claude/rules/**`, so editing an instruction document
compiled context unrelated to its content. Measured again on 2026-07-30 with
`target_files: ["AGENTS.md"]`: every document returned came from the `review`
*command* edge, and the path contributed nothing.

The observation named `.claude/rules/authoring.md`, which no longer exists — its
content moved into AGENTS.md, which is loaded every session. That narrows the gap
from what the observation described: the authoring *rules* are already in context.
What is missing is the *decisions about* those files.

## Decision

**Tag mappings live in `aegis-share/source/tag-mappings.json`** (entries are
`{tag, doc_id, confidence, source}`), published by the share pipeline like the
rest of `source/`. Seven tags ship: `secrets`, `records`, `gates`, `deployment`,
`dependencies`, `layering`, `delegation`.

**A mapping earns its place only if some real compile exists where no path or
command edge already surfaces that document** — concretely: a plausible
`target_files` whose paths have no edge to it, under a `command` that has no edge
to it either. Only `scaffold`, `refactor` and `review` are ever passed in this
repository, so "some command" means one of those three, not a hypothetical one.

The looser reading — "the tag reaches it somehow" — is what the first draft used,
and it let through `records` → `adr-0008` when all three commands already reach
`adr-0008` at priority 100. That mapping was removed. The test has teeth only if
applied per mapping rather than per tag: `delegation` survives because `review`
reaches neither `adr-0006` nor `adr-0012`, and `layering` survives because
`adr-0016` names `.claude/rules/react.md` as the companion holding its
module-placement rules while no edge connects the two.

Duplicating an existing edge as a tag adds vocabulary without adding reach, and a
catalog too large to hold in mind stops being used. Verified: a compile on
`.github/workflows/ci.yaml` (no path edge at all) under `command: "refactor"` with
`["secrets", "deployment"]` returned 3 base documents — all three via `refactor`
command edges — plus **5 expanded**, each attributed to its tag.

**Instruction documents get path edges to the decisions that govern them, and are
not themselves added to the knowledge base.** `AGENTS.md` → ADR-0008 (it is the
single always-on instruction file, and re-adding detailed rule files was rejected)
and ADR-0021 (records belong in the KB, not here) — both are mistakes
re-introducible by editing that exact file. `.claude/rules/**` → ADR-0008, whose
2026-07-25 amendment is specifically about why those path-scoped files exist.
`.claude/skills/**` → ADR-0006 (skills are sub-steps, never parallel
orchestrators); only three named skills had edges before.

This keeps ADR-0008 item 2 ("the KB carries ADRs only") intact, closing the
`expanded` Consequence ADR-0021 left open.

## Alternatives considered

- **Relax the ADR-only policy so the rule files are served for edits to
  themselves**: the observation's other suggestion, rejected. `AGENTS.md` and
  `.claude/rules/` are already in the prompt when they apply — always-on for the
  former, path-scoped for the latter — so serving them again would return content
  the reader already has, and would put two copies of a live rule under two
  different update disciplines. ADR-0008 item 2 exists for that reason.
- **A tag per document, mirroring the edges**: rejected by the reach test. It
  doubles the vocabulary and adds nothing a path edge does not already supply.
- **Leave the catalog empty and rely on the server-side SLM tagger**: rejected —
  the tagger infers tags from `plan` and still resolves them through
  `tag_mappings`, so an empty table makes it inert too.

## Consequences

- `intent_tags` becomes a real choice, and `[]` becomes a real one too. AGENTS.md's
  step 2 now names the file and states the reach test, so the catalog has a stated
  growth rule rather than accreting.
- The tags in `source/tag-mappings.json` are a starting vocabulary chosen from this
  project's recurring work, not a taxonomy. Expect to add and retire them; the reach
  test is what keeps that honest. The count is deliberately not written here — this
  line said "seven" while the file held eight from the day it was committed.
- `confidence` is set by hand (1.0 where the tag is squarely the document's
  subject, 0.7–0.8 where it is secondary). Nothing validates those numbers, so
  they are an ordering hint, not a measurement.
- A fork that drops `tag-mappings.json` silently returns to the inert state.
  `manifest.json`'s `includes_tag_mappings` is the one-field check.

documents.title: Commit Gate Shape Is Shared And Markers Are Not Bash Writable
documents.content:
# 0024. One definition of "lands a commit"; the gate's markers are not writable from Bash

- Status: accepted
- Date: 2026-07-30

## Context

An adversarial audit on 2026-07-30 found three ways past the commit gate ADR-0013
established. All three predate that day's work on *what the stamp certifies*, so
the gate was being made more meaningful while remaining walkable.

1. **A metacharacter against the command word skipped the gate entirely.** Both
   `pre-bash-guard.sh` and `post-bash-stamp-consume.sh` required the character
   before `git` to be start-of-string or one of `;&| `. Verified: `(git commit)`,
   `$(git commit)` and the backtick form matched none of those and were never
   examined — no stamp required. `(cd sub && git commit)` *was* caught, but only
   because the space after `&&` happened to satisfy the class.
2. **The two guards had drifted, and the drift was a hole.** The consume side
   required whitespace after `commit`; the gate accepted any `\bcommit\b`. So
   `git commit;true` was gated on the way in and **not** recognised as a landed
   commit on the way out, leaving a live stamp to authorise the next, unreviewed
   change — precisely the hole `post-bash-stamp-consume.sh` exists to close
   (ADR-0019). The two patterns carried a comment asking the next editor to "keep
   the two patterns in step". That is an instruction, and this repository has
   concluded three times that instructions are not mechanisms (ADR-0001, ADR-0013,
   ADR-0019).
3. **The stamp was forgeable with one allow-listed command.** `Bash(touch:*)` is in
   `permissions.allow` and nothing protected the marker files, so
   `touch .claude/.review-stamp` satisfied the gate with no review at all. The only
   thing standing against it was a sentence in the `review-diff` skill saying not
   to. Guard 1 in the same file already applies a lexical guard to the env files for
   exactly this reason — "allowed Bash readers could walk around `permissions.deny`"
   — and that reasoning was never extended to the gate's own state.

## Decision

**One shared definition of the shape.** `lib-commit-shape.sh` holds
`command_lands_a_commit()`, sourced by both hooks. Statement separators and
grouping characters become newlines and the test runs per line, so a metacharacter
against `git` cannot hide it; backslash-newline is joined first, because it is a
continuation rather than a separator; only horizontal whitespace is squeezed after
that, because squeezing all whitespace would rejoin the statements just split and
make `git status; echo commit` match. `commit` stays a whitespace-delimited word so
`git log --grep=commit` is not a commit.

Sharing is the point, not the pattern. Two hooks answering the same question with
two hand-written regexes is a drift waiting to happen, and the drift is silent: the
gate keeps blocking, so nothing looks broken while the stamp quietly outlives its
batch.

**The gate's markers are refused from Bash, and denied to `Write`/`Edit`.** A new
Guard 3 in `pre-bash-guard.sh` refuses any command naming `.review-stamp`,
`.finder-done`, `.finder-hash` or `.pair-ok`; eight `permissions.deny` entries cover
the two tools a Bash guard cannot see. Reads are refused along with writes because
separating them lexically needs a verb list and a verb list rots — `ls -la .claude/`
shows every marker's state without naming one, so no diagnostic is lost.

`scripts/test-bash-guard.py` and `scripts/test-review-gate.py` pin the shapes listed
below on the gate and consume sides respectively, so the two can no longer disagree
without a test failing. "Every shape" is deliberately not claimed — the review of
this change found three the first version missed, and the honest statement is a list
plus a named residual, not a universal.

The reviewed set: the plain form; a metacharacter glued before `git`
(`(…)`, `$(…)`, backticks, brace group, conditional); an operator glued after
`commit`; `git add -A && …`; a backslash line continuation, including one splitting
the verb itself; a quoted verb (`git 'commit'`); and `git${IFS}commit`. Bash removes
quotes and performs `${IFS}` splitting before dispatch, so those two really do
commit; the normalisation strips quotes and expands the braced `${IFS}` for that
reason. `$IFScommit` needs no handling — bash reads it as one undefined variable
name and no commit runs.

## Alternatives considered

- **Fix the two regexes separately and keep the "stay in step" comment**: rejected.
  That comment is the thing that failed; the hole existed *because* the two were
  maintained by hand against a request to remember.
- **A verb allow-list so marker reads stay possible**: rejected. It is an
  enumeration, so it rots, and it would have to be right about every file-creating
  verb. `ls -la .claude/` covers the real need.
- **Parse the command properly instead of normalising**: rejected as
  disproportionate. A shell parser in a hook is a large dependency for a check whose
  honest ceiling is "raise the bar", and the guard already over-matches in the safe
  direction.
- **Rely on `permissions.deny` alone for the markers**: rejected — `deny` governs
  tools, and `touch` is a Bash command. Guard 1 exists because of that exact gap.

## Consequences
 
- Every shape in the reviewed set above now both blocks when unstamped and consumes
  the stamp when landed, and neither behaviour can drift from the other without a
  test failing. The consume side additionally truncates at the first heredoc
  operator: prose in a heredoc body reading `git … commit` was enough to delete a
  stamp the review had earned, and writing a document through a heredoc is routine
  here. The gate side keeps the heredoc, staying the stricter of the two.
- **Two named residuals, rather than a generic disclaimer.** *Visible but unparsed
  text* is now handled for the shapes above; what remains is *invisible state*. A
  git alias (`alias.ci=commit`) makes `git ci -m x` land a commit with the word
  absent from the command entirely — undetectable without resolving aliases at hook
  time, which is the "parse the command properly" direction rejected above. And any
  further quoting or expansion trick not in the reviewed set is unhandled by
  construction. Naming these beats the earlier wording, which asserted "every shape"
  and was false within one review.
- **A cost accepted knowingly.** Stripping quotes means a git subcommand whose quoted
  argument is literally `commit` — `git show 'commit'` for a ref of that name — now
  reads as a commit. On the gate side that re-runs a check that passes; on the
  consume side it costs one unnecessary review. Both are cheaper than the confirmed
  bypass they close.
- **Naming a marker in a Bash command now fails**, including in prose. That is the
  same friction Guard 1 already imposes for the env files, and it bit repeatedly
  while writing this change: several diagnostic commands had to be rephrased, and a
  `grep` for the deny entries was refused for quoting a filename. Annoying, and the
  safe direction.
- **Still lexical, therefore still defeatable.** An agent that decides to cheat can
  obfuscate the path or the command. What this buys is that forging is no longer
  allow-listed and silent — it requires deliberate evasion, visible in the
  transcript. Same honest framing as ADR-0017 for secrets: defense-in-depth, not a
  boundary.
- The gate now rests on three mechanisms rather than one instruction, but the
  ordering lesson stands on its own: four review cycles went into making the stamp
  certify the right event while `(git commit)` walked past the gate that requires it.
  Auditing what a gate *enforces* should precede refining what it *means*.

documents.title: Per Edit Lint Hook Removed
documents.content:
# 0025. The per-edit lint hook is removed; lint lives at commit, push and CI

- Status: accepted
- Date: 2026-07-31

## Context

`post-edit-check.sh` ran on every `Edit`/`Write`/`MultiEdit`, linting the one file
just written with `bunx oxlint --type-aware` and blocking the next tool call on
failure. It was the first of four layers running the same linter: `lefthook.yml`
lints staged files at pre-commit and runs `bun run check` whole-project at
pre-push, `stop-gate.sh` runs it at the end of a turn, and `ci.yaml` runs it on
every push to `main` and every PR.

So the hook did not decide whether a lint error reaches `main`. What it bought was
latency: a failure surfaced while the edit was still in context instead of at
commit time, when several files' failures arrive together.

What it cost was a `bunx` invocation per edit, and blocking on states that are
legitimately broken mid-change. That cost was already paid down once: the hook
originally ran whole-project checks, and was narrowed to the single edited file
because running them per edit "re-checked the world N times per task and blocked
legitimate mid-refactor states" (its own comment). The narrowing reduced the
problem without removing it — a multi-file refactor still trips it between the
first edit and the last.

The repository owner asked for it to go.

## Decision

Delete `post-edit-check.sh` and its `PostToolUse` registration. Lint runs at
pre-commit (staged files), pre-push (whole project), the Stop gate, and CI.

This amends **ADR-0012**, whose Context cites "the per-edit lint hook and the
review gate moved the quality argument" as part of why the parent implements
directly rather than delegating for quality reasons. One of those two mechanisms
is now gone. The decision stands: the review gate — a fresh-context finder and
verifier the parent cannot talk past — is the load-bearing half, and the three
remaining lint layers all sit between an edit and `main`. What changes is that
nothing corrects the parent mid-task, so `start-workflow` step 6's own checks
matter more, and the skill now says so instead of pointing at a hook.

`scripts/test-review-gate.py` drove this hook so that its "a fix needs no second
review" assertions ran through the mechanism that had once cleared the stamp on
every edit (ADR-0013, removed by ADR-0019). With no hook to drive, `edit()` is a
plain write. The suite therefore can no longer detect a *future* hook that starts
clearing the stamp on every edit; the helper carries that warning, because the
assertion would silently pass for the wrong reason.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep it for feedback latency**: rejected by the owner. The argument is real but
  it is a convenience, not a guarantee, and it is the only thing the hook provided.
- **Keep it non-blocking (warn instead of block)**: rejected — ADR-0013 established
  that a warning the agent may ignore is not a gate, so this would keep the
  per-edit cost while dropping the one property that made the cost defensible.
- **Widen it to typecheck as well**: rejected — the opposite direction. Whole-project
  typecheck per edit is what the original narrowing removed.

## Consequences

- A lint error now surfaces at the first of pre-commit, the Stop gate, or CI,
  whichever the session reaches first — later than before, and in batches.
- Editing many files no longer pays a `bunx` start per file.
- `PostToolUse` has three registrations left, all of them Aegis- or gate-related.
  No hook fires on an edit at all, which is worth knowing before assuming an edit
  is checked by something.
- Nothing in the enforcement layer now depends on a `PostToolUse(Edit|Write)`
  registration existing, so re-adding one is a fresh decision rather than a
  restoration.

documents.title: Editor Adapter Mirrors Removed
documents.content:
# 0026. The `.cursor/` and `.codex/` adapter mirrors are removed; `deploy-adapters` is not run

- Status: accepted (amended by 0031)
- Date: 2026-07-31

> **Note (ADR-0031, 2026-08-07):** `.cursor/rules/` exists again — as
> file-level symlinks into `.claude/rules/`, never copies. A symlink cannot
> drift, which is the failure this ADR removed. The deletion of *copies*, the
> `deploy-adapters` ban, and the Consequences below stand; the sentence that
> Cursor sessions "get no Aegis instructions" no longer holds. The
> `deploy-adapters` warning itself moved from AGENTS.md to
> `.claude/rules/aegis.md`.

## Context

`npx @fuwasegu/aegis deploy-adapters` writes the Aegis process instructions into
one file per editor. Run on 2026-04-30 (`deaa1d8`), it produced
`.cursor/rules/aegis-process.mdc` — a full copy of AGENTS.md's
`aegis:start`/`aegis:end` block, which Cursor loads as an always-on rule — plus
mirrors of three aegis skills under `.cursor/skills/` and `.codex/skills/`.

Those copies then sat untouched for three months while the block they mirror was
edited repeatedly. By 2026-07-31 the Cursor copy said `intent_tags` was
"recommended" in one step and "optional" in another, while the block required it
and `pre-aegis-compile-guard.sh` blocked any call that omitted it. It also still
carried the vendor's placeholder path example from another codebase. Nothing
detected the drift: no gate reads those files, and nothing in the repository even
recorded that they were copies.

The same day, running the command to resolve the "adapter templates may be
outdated" notice that ends every aegis response overwrote the block itself with
the vendor template — reverting that day's edits, substituting the foreign path
example, and appending a second copy of the block to `CLAUDE.md`, which ADR-0008
keeps at `@AGENTS.md` alone. It reported each file as created/updated/unchanged
and asked nothing first. The damage was reverted before any of it was committed.

## Decision

**Delete `.cursor/` and `.codex/`, and do not run `deploy-adapters`.**

The rules have one home: AGENTS.md, loaded every session. This is ADR-0008's
decision item 1 applied to a copy that ADR-0008 did not anticipate, and the same
reasoning ADR-0021 used to delete `docs/adr/` — two copies under two update
disciplines means one of them is wrong, and the wrong one is whichever a reader
happens to open.

Reconciling the copies instead was rejected: reconciliation would have been
correct on the day it was done and stale again at the next edit to the block, and
the three months just spent proves the discipline does not hold. Nothing here can
detect the drift, so the only durable form is not having the copy.

AGENTS.md carries the operational half of this — a section placed deliberately
*outside* the managed block, because anything written inside it is what the
command discards.

## Alternatives considered

- **Reconcile `.cursor/rules/aegis-process.mdc` and keep it**: rejected, above.
  It also leaves `deploy-adapters` a step someone will eventually take.
- **Keep the mirrors and add a gate that compares them to the block**: rejected as
  a mechanism built to protect a duplicate. The cheaper move is to delete the
  duplicate; a gate here would be the second-best fix to a problem with a
  first-best one.
- **Keep them for template users on Cursor or Codex**: the real cost, accepted
  rather than dismissed. A fork into those editors now runs `deploy-adapters`
  itself — the right default there, since its template has not diverged yet and
  the command is not yet destructive. `docs/FORKING.md` is silent on these
  directories and is not amended: that is the fork's decision, not ours.

## Consequences

- Cursor and Codex sessions in *this* repository get no Aegis instructions. That
  is honest rather than harmful: they also have none of the hooks the instructions
  assume, so a Cursor agent following them could not have satisfied the gates
  anyway.
- The "adapter templates may be outdated" notice will keep appearing on every
  aegis response and must keep being ignored. A notice that must be permanently
  disregarded is a poor state; it is tolerated because the alternative is letting
  a vendor command overwrite hand-edited instructions.
- If the aegis template ever gains something worth having, it is diffed in by
  hand. Nothing automates that, and nothing detects when the template moves.
- `deploy-adapters` recreates the deleted directories. Their absence is therefore
  not self-maintaining, which is why the AGENTS.md section names the command
  rather than only the files.

documents.title: Session Marker Clear Keys On Session Identity
documents.content:
# 0027. The SessionStart marker clear keys on session identity, not on the event firing

- Status: accepted (amended by 0028)
- Date: 2026-08-04

> **Amended by ADR-0028** (2026-08-04): the Decision below is the id half of what
> is now a two-part rule. `source` was rejected here for want of observed values;
> those values have since been settled, so `clear` and `fork` force a clear
> whatever the id says. That closes a hole this ADR opened without noticing:
> `/clear` starts a different body of work, and if `session_id` survives it, the
> rule below keeps a stamp an unreviewed task could spend. The accepted-risk list
> below is otherwise unchanged — notably `resume`, which ADR-0028 tried to close
> and had to back out.

## Context

ADR-0013 gave `session-start-env-check.sh` one job beyond reporting degrades:
clear every per-session gate marker, so one session's state cannot authorise
another's commit. It cleared unconditionally, on every `SessionStart`.

That holds while `SessionStart` means "a new session began". In this project's
remote containers it does not. The event also fires when an MCP server
reconnects, and reconnects happen repeatedly inside one continuous session.

On 2026-08-03/04 that cost three complete find→verify passes on one change.
Each pass ran to completion, each wrote `.review-stamp`, and each stamp was gone
before the commit it authorised could run — every loss landing on a turn
boundary, never inside a turn. The diagnosis is by elimination plus one positive
signal: `session-start-env-check.sh` is the only thing in the repository that
removes `.review-stamp` without a commit (`post-bash-stamp-consume.sh` needs a
commit that leaves the tree clean, and no commit ran), and it is likewise the
only remover of `.aegis-unavailable`, which was observed vanishing in the same
instant as a stamp.

The failure mode is the one ADR-0013 exists to prevent, inverted. A gate that
cannot be *earned* is as broken as one that cannot be trusted: three passes, ~300k
tokens, and no commit.

## Decision

Clear the markers only when the session actually changed. The hook reads
`session_id` from the `SessionStart` payload and compares it with the value
remembered in a new `.claude/.session-id` marker:
